articles.title: An MLA recited the whole of Psalm 103 to her in Telugu, and she went to the ladies' restroom and cried
articles.deck: She had been a Crusader, then Legion of Mary, then twenty-five years in the Christian Workers Movement. She was a nominated Member of the Legislative Assembly. And she could not name a single Bible reference.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published from the May-July 2014 issue, pages 4 to 6, where it ran unsigned as the cover story. The biographical section was written by the magazine and appears here under the magazine's byline; the testimony that follows it is in her own words, as the 2014 page said. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected. Her surname is given here as the magazine had it, Lazares, which is also the spelling she uses herself; independent press coverage and the Legislative Assembly record spell it Lazarus. The 2014 page ended with her personal email address and website, which have not been reproduced. Most of the biographical claims below could not be independently verified in 2026 and are presented as the magazine's account of 2014 rather than as established fact.

body.v: Christine Skinner Lazares of Hyderabad was a nominated Member of the Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh, serving three terms from 1989, and founded the Anglo-Indian Welfare Association of A.P. This profile is the magazine's own account as published in 2014. Where it makes claims about her family and her awards, those are as she gave them and have not been independently confirmed since.

Christine Skinner Lazares is the eldest daughter of the late Doris and Reuben Skinner of the famed Skinner's Horse. As a child Christine harboured the dream of being a nurse like her grandmother Mary Skinner, who served as Matron to the Nizam's family. However, her innate sense of caring and strong urge to do social good led her on a different path. As a fourth-generation Hyderabadi, she is proud of her Telangana heritage and roots. To some extent her story maps the trajectory of India's newest state.

A highly resourceful individual, Christine optimised her degree in Business Management to reach a managerial position with the Hyderabad-based Pest Control India Pvt. Ltd., where she started working at a very young age. At thirty-five, with fifteen years of service behind her and despite being a mother of two, she pursued a degree in Management Studies, which was deemed mandatory for her to take up a promotion.
Nineteen, and already a Joint Secretary

Inspired by parents who instilled strong ideals of social justice and community service in her, Christine was involved at a very young age in leadership roles with the Crusaders at the Legion of Mary. Her nature was so moulded to public service issues that at the age of nineteen she was appointed the first Joint Secretary for the Council of Hansen's Social Welfare, and serves as its Chairperson to this day.

During her work there she fought hard to procure land allotment for leprosy patients and helped establish the CHSW Centre at Parvatnagar, aided by LEPRA India. She was recognised for that work with a lifetime achievement award from the Governor of Andhra Pradesh in 2009.

A gregarious extrovert, Christine served in several organisations providing services to young and disabled people before she began focusing on the needs of the Anglo-Indian community. In recognition of her work for the disadvantaged, she was nominated as an MLA for the first time for the 1989 to 1994 term by the Governor of Andhra Pradesh. She championed the cause of the Anglo-Indian community by establishing the Anglo-Indian Welfare Association.
What she actually did with the seat

Among her other accomplishments are the setting up of YMCA and YWCA programmes by aligning them with the Department of Industries. She worked with the Government of Andhra Pradesh to set up Aashray, a home for children in distress. She convened seminars on alcoholism, to help both alcoholics and the families affected by it, in her capacity as Convenor of the Joint Action Forum of Women. She also set up government vocational training for women through the small industries service institute at the YMCA.

She is a founding member of the United Christmas Celebrations. In that role she demanded a Christian Finance Corporation, so that budget allocations are spent for the community and enhancement funds accrue regularly. She was instrumental in ensuring that Christmas is celebrated in every district, and not restricted to a High Tea with the Chief Minister in Hyderabad.

Religion is a sticky wicket for any politician, but Christine took the bull by the horns in order to address the accusation against the Church of selling properties illegally. She was tenacious in her efforts with the government to protect, restore and retrieve any lands allocated to the Church on religious grounds. Along with the House Committee she prepared legislation on the matter, which she says has since been relegated to the back burner.

Due to her efforts, 185 professional seats were allotted to the Anglo-Indian community. As always, there were a few who did not fully understand her mission, but she did not let their hesitation stop her from doing what she believed was right.
The salvation experience, in her own words

I was born into a family where my mother, who was Anglican, had to become a Catholic to marry my father, who in those times was Cambridge educated and excelled in religious studies. As a voracious reader his conversation with my mother was kind of banned, but I gleaned much from their heated arguments about why we children should not read the Bible.

My grandfather, an army man, was also a dedicated Catholic, and ever since I can remember, all the children from the compound had to get up early in the morning to walk to church before Mass to wipe the benches, later to cut flowers for the altar, graduating to polishing the brass and singing in the choir.

In school I was a Crusader and then graduated to the Legion of Mary, and after marriage to a staunch Catholic I served the Christian Workers Movement for more than twenty-five years. But those arguments were in the back of my mind, and I kept searching for the answers to my questions.
Ask me anything from the Bible

It was in my first term as an MLA. All members requested assistance with admissions in various schools and colleges, but one told me he was a Christian. Taken aback, I replied, "Yes, all are Christian when they want something." He said, ask me anything from the Bible.
For a long minute I was perturbed. I did not know a reference.
For a long minute I was perturbed. I did not know a reference.
body.highlight: I did not know a reference

body.v: My mother had the habit of singing psalms, and would quote the number. Thank God, that morning she had sung Psalm 103. I recalled it and said, all right, recite 103, thinking in the back of my mind that this man was trying something new to get my attention. During the first term that was a great problem.

But the MLA recited every word in Telugu, with so much passion. Tears welled up in my eyes and I went to the ladies' restroom and cried my heart out. I said, O my God, I am a Christian, my name is Christine, and I am lost.

It was then I promised myself I would study the Bible, and from all through those years of the first term until today I started to pray, and went to nearly every church and home prayer meeting, and belong to many prayer groups.
You will be the first Catholic

At the last meeting of my first term I was invited as chief guest to Andhra Christian Theological College at Lower Tank Bund for a youth meet, and narrated my story: the questions I had had as a young person, and that there was no Catholic Bible college.
The Principal interrupted me and said, you are most welcome at ACTC. I replied, but I am a Catholic. To which he replied, you will be the first Catholic.
I replied, but I am a Catholic. To which he replied, you will be the first Catholic.
body.highlight: you will be the first Catholic

body.v: I was elated, and asked if I could join in the year 1995. I did, and completed a four-year Bachelor in Christian Studies that answered all of my questions. I found answers to who I am and what God wanted from me, and most of all I learned the lessons on righteousness and justice.

Once a Catholic, always one. But my entire perspective on life changed, and most of the time I had the church leadership by the horns, totally upset with me for raising the issue of the illegal sale of Christian properties. I made legislation for the protection, revival, restoration and rebuilding of thousands of acres of properties that did not see the light of day, with vociferous condemnation from the elders.
Today I count one loss: of our presence as Christians in the land. Our dignity. Our integrity. And with it the only opportunity of participating in the Great Commission.

articles.title: David did not start out fighting giants. He started out with smelly, stupid sheep where nobody could see him
articles.deck: Part two. Most people want the giant opportunity now and are not patient enough to be faithful in the small things. A pastor who spent his first seventeen years in churches of under three hundred on what that time was for.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the May-July 2014 issue, pages 8 and 9, as the second part of the article begun in March-April. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is the author's throughout. One claim in it is not a fact and is addressed in a note at the foot.

body.v: In the last issue of 5Talents I introduced the topic of facing the giants in your life. They may not be literal giants like the one David faced, who stood over nine feet tall, but we face them nonetheless, and they come in all shapes and sizes.

We took a look at three giant statements about giants. Every giant introduces a person to himself. People who are growing to their highest potential have defeated giants. And giants are often tools God uses to shape us for even bigger things.

So, like David, how can we effectively face our giants and keep them from deterring us from realizing our full potential in both our personal and professional life? This month I'll begin by sharing the first of several steps.
Be faithful in the little things
Not every giant is a problem that has to be overcome. Some are actually opportunities that can be doorways to bigger things.

David was the youngest of eight brothers. The three oldest were on the battle lines, and David had the responsibility of going back and forth from tending his father's sheep to delivering supplies to his brothers.

Though he was the youngest, he was not the dumbest. He had the military mind of a Colin Powell, the political savvy of a nation's President, the athletic skill of a Milkha Singh, and the musical ability of Beethoven, all wrapped up into one.
Yet where did David spend most of his time? Not on the front lines facing the enemy, but in the backwoods caring for smelly, stupid sheep where no one would ever see him.
Not on the front lines facing the enemy, but in the backwoods caring for smelly, stupid sheep where no one would ever see him.
body.highlight: where no one would ever see him

body.v: Think about this. Did David ever whine and complain because he wasn't in the war zone? No. Did David ever accuse God of overlooking him? No. Did David throw a pity party and complain that he never got any breaks? No.

David didn't start out fighting giants on the battlefield, he started out tending sheep on the hillside. David didn't start out as a soldier fighting for Saul, he started out as a musician soothing Saul.

He was faithful in the little things and doing what he was supposed to be doing, obeying his dad, tending the sheep, and practicing his music. David knew that God was preparing him for bigger and better things. But during this time he was getting to know God. During this time God was developing his character. During this time God was preparing him.
Forged in the private place

Many people want a giant opportunity right now but aren't patient enough to be faithful in the little things. However, before we can take on bigger and tougher giants, our character, abilities, and talents are forged in the little things and most often in the private places. That's because who we really are is forged in the private place, not the public arena.

So where are you today? Are you aspiring to be a great leader? To own your own company? To run your own business? To influence the lives of many? That's a great dream and a noble ambition. By all means, hold on to it. But remember, it starts with the small things, the little things that don't seem as important.
Seventeen years in small churches

I pastor a great church and have the joy and responsibility of teaching several thousand every weekend. But it hasn't always been that way. My first 17 years of ministry were in churches all numbering less than 300.

Now I have the opportunity of travelling and speaking to groups nationally and internationally several times a year. Once in a while someone will say something like, "I wish I could do what you do." The question I am asking on the inside is, "Are you willing to do what I've done?"
Once in a while someone will say, "I wish I could do what you do." The question I am asking on the inside is, "Are you willing to do what I've done?"
body.highlight: Are you willing to do what I've done

body.v: Most don't start out facing the big giants. They start out tackling the smaller ones.
But be faithful. Do your job and do your best. Be faithful in the little things and trust God to give you the opportunity for greater responsibility in His time.

One note on a claim in this piece. The line giving David an IQ of 150, which appeared in the 2014 issue, has not been reproduced: no figure of that kind exists or could exist for a Bronze Age figure, and it is a preaching commonplace rather than a fact. The comparison to Colin Powell, Milkha Singh and Beethoven is the author's own and is kept. Readers may also notice that Milkha Singh is the one Indian name in a list of Western examples, which suggests the piece was adapted for this magazine's readership.
